The WXYZ article speaks about Dr Brumley, State Superintendent, coming to Shelby County to check up on the progress of installation of cameras inside special education classrooms. The addition of cameras in these classrooms started with requests from parents and has been funded through laws passed in the Louisiana legislature. 
In chapter 2 of the textbook, we see that one of the important administrative duties is to make sure that discrimination of special education students does not occur. With the accountability that these camera devices will provide, this move will serve as a deterrent to discrimination and enforce that services are being provided daily.
In addition, Chapter 7 describes the procedures for handling discipline with students who have a disability. Having a resource such as a camera inside of the classroom will help administration make sure that the proper punishment fits the offense. Administrators must be careful with out of school placements due to an exceptional student who has behavior problems. Not only will it help with this effort on the administrative level, it will also help with classroom discipline as the teachers and parents will be held accountable for their actions with the student in their care.
Chapter 8 talks extensively about parental rights when it comes to students who have disabilities. The right to a camera in the classroom has been established by the government. If a parent has requested that a camera be placed in the classroom it must be placed. This entire effort was put into motion by parental request; therefore it is simply just another safeguard and accountability measure for parents to ensure that their children are being best cared for.
As far as the legislation that Dr. Brumley has spoken about in this article, the best steps for an administrator to take is to follow suit if any parent requests a camera be placed inside of their self-contained student’s classroom. Not only will this resource provide accountability measures across the board, it can also foster goodwill with those in the community who have students receiving accommodations. However, it is quite important that the teachers who are delivering these services  not feel as though they are being spied upon by administration. It would be a very wise thing to have frank and honest discussions with staff and faculty on the reasons that these cameras exist in the first place.
Fairview High School is nestled in east Monroe County and is located in between the larger cities of Springfield and Centerville.  Camp Williams, (formerly Camp Bradley,) is also near this K-12 class C school that contains all grade levels under one roof.  Fairview is well known in the area for the prowess of both girls and boys basketball, as well as the accolades received from track and field.  Fairview itself is a small country municipality that does not qualify for a township moniker, and instead is classified as a village boasting a population of 549 according to 2024 census data. (World Population Review, 2024)
	Like many small schools, Fairview is the epicenter of activities for the entire village.  Most community events are centered around school activities and athletic events.  If you come to Fairview on a game night, you might be led to believe no one lives there, because all vehicles would be parked at, and families would be inside, Fairview High’s gymnasium.  Many family dinners are provided by way of nachos sold through the gymnasium concession stand.
	At the helm of Fairview High School is second year principal, Mrs.
M .  Mrs. M came to Fairview High 4 years ago and served two years as the assistant principal before taking over the reins of the school through promotion after the former principal was reassigned to another principalship in the district.  Fairview High School and the surrounding community is quite idyllic, and Mrs. M intends to maintain this environment by keeping a keen eye on updated school laws and meticulously following ethical standards in the way that she treats both students and others.  The three areas of major concern for her in this regard are navigating the laws surrounding students receiving special education accommodations, properly disciplining students, and correcting the behavior of personnel.  In the educational realm, the ever-changing landscape of law and ethics makes this a challenge for administrators no matter what their years of experience.  
Challenge 1: The Special Education Student
	By in large, Principal M feels that the biggest challenge that administrators must face is understanding the rights and protections that are afforded to students that qualify for special education services.  She states that this population of students has so many rights, and in her words, administrators “must get it right” when dealing with a SPED student. (Miller, 2024)  A major concern is the ever-looming threat of litigation being pursued if an administrator violates the rights of these students.  
	Since Simpon High is such a small school it has limited resources and thus not able to provide all SPED services that other schools may be able to give.  All their SPED services are conducted almost inclusively in the classroom as they do not have specific seclusion classrooms to pull students out of the regular classroom environments.  Fairview High does have an 80/20 split available for special education students that they utilize daily if needed in which 20 percent of the educational time is spent one-on-one outside of the regular classroom setting to give tutoring and occupational supports.  Those students that require a majority seclusion type services are simply navigated to larger schools nearby that can adequately provide the needed accommodations.  According to Principal M, it is against the law to deny SPED services to a student that qualifies for them, so instead of enrolling a student needing services that they cannot provide, they consult district level administrators and find ways to get the student to the nearest school that can fully meet their needs. (Miller, 2024)  Principal M relates a story of a student that recently desired to enroll at Fairview High School but couldn’t because their needs wouldn’t be met.  The school board setup appropriate transportation from Fairview to another school where they happily enrolled and received all services needed.  
	Another area that affects the way administration handles a student with special education accommodations is dealing with disciplinary issues.  The law dictates certain parameters when it comes to suspending or expelling special education students.  One such parameter is that even if a student has been suspended or expelled, the special education student must continue to receive the services that they are due. (Yell, 2023)  In addition, there are limits on the days of overall suspensions allowed when they stem from a pattern of similar behavior, as well as protections for the student if the misbehavior is attributed to their disability.  Special meetings, or manifestation hearings, are used to determine if a student’s specific disability is the source of the unwanted behavior, and if determined that they are the cause, the student cannot be subject for further disciplinary action for that manifestation.  On one hand, this seems difficult for administrators, however considerations must be given to the student that is receiving SPED services while at school to help deal with these misbehaviors.
	In addition, Principal M has found that many teachers applying accommodations for special education students may not be aware of all the changes in the law that inevitably are modified each year.  The issue that she encounters is the classic ideology of “this is the way we’ve always done things,” when it comes to modifying practices to stay within the confines of new legislation.  She relates that this is her primary area of concern due to having to overcome entrenched practices and making things right for her SPED students.
Challenge #2: Behavior Issues
	Although this may fall under more of an ethical quandry, Principal M relates that another area of concern for her personally is dealing with student discipline and being fair to each student that is involved.  She is meticulous in her investigations of alleged wrongdoing because she wants to be sure that she gets each disciplinary case correct.  She relates that she doesn’t want to discipline a student and “later find out they are innocent.” (Miller, 2024)  
	This idea of gathering evidence is called due process and is undergirded by educational law.  An administrator cannot discipline a student without evidence to support an allegation of wrongdoing.  “Can a school punish you without evidence? The answer is no, as schools are required to follow due process rights to ensure fair treatment. Understanding these rights empowers students and parents to protect themselves from unjust disciplinary actions.” (educationlawyers.com, n.d.)
	The landmark case that is referenced in due process issues is Goss vs. Lopez involving a group of students that were suspended in Columbus, Ohio in 1975.  This case appeared before the Supreme Court of the United States in which the court ruled that the fourteenth amendment rights of a group of students were violated because they were suspended by a school without due process. (DeCooman, 2023)  Nine students were suspended and “none were given any type of hearing or notification of their behaviors considered grounds for suspension, as a form of procedural due process.” (DeCooman, 2023)  It is clear why Principal Miller takes due diligence when it comes to student discipline, especially when it comes to idea of suspension, or other actions that could limit a student’s right to education.  
	In addition, Principal M relates that bullying by students in on the rise but is quite hard to prove.  Many cases that are handled end in a stale mate with one student’s words against another with a lack of evidence that can help administrators decide one way or the other.  Besides the lack of evidence that often accompany these cases, she states that bullying cases are hardly reported in Fairview’s small school environment.  If bullying is occurring, then quite often students aren’t letting teachers know.
Challenge #3: Personnel
	School administration is also tasked with the responsibility of helping teachers remain successful in the classroom.  Sometimes this takes the form of professional development and equipping teachers with the latest skills and other times it is guiding teachers that are not following proper protocols and procedures.  The final concern brought up by Principal M was the ethics involved with handling undesired actions or attitudes of teachers.  Author Edgar Rice Burroughs stated, "We are, all of us, creatures of habit, and when the seeming necessity for schooling ourselves in new ways ceases to exist, we fall naturally and easily into the manner and customs which long usage has implanted ineradicably within us".  Once a person establishes a routine, it can be hard to break from those routines and adjust methodologies to better meet student needs and adhere to new educational mandates.  
	Principal M is no stranger to handling personnel issues and has a unique take on handling school level issues that arise when a teacher may need corrective action in this area.  When she identifies an area that a teacher needs to correct, she brings them in to hold a conference.  If afterward it appears that the adjustments were not made, she brings them in and writes them up and establishes written expectations to be signed by both parties.  According to Principal M, her intentions are to help protect the teacher by documenting these actions at the school level so that if district personnel were to ever question a situation, documentation would exist that shows the situation handled.  However, Principal M states that most of these interactions are not seen in this light by the teachers.  She says that most become belligerent at the corrective action and then claim that they are being harassed.  What she intends as protection, according to her, is taken as harassment.
	Harassment is a serious accusation to make against a supervisor and one that needs to have documentable evidence to prove.  According to legal experts, harassment includes things such as inappropriate comments, unwelcomed touching, offensive gestures, mocking, suggestive eye contact, derogatory remarks, threatening comments, overly personal questions, and other things like offensive cartoon posters.  (Manes, 2017)  Natural human emotions cause many to become defensive when confronted with a perceived wrong.  This innate sense of humanity coupled with a tense situation can become a catalyst for these types of complaints from subordinates.  Principal M says that administration must navigate these waters carefully by documenting all unwanted behavior and corrective actions given, as well as updating notes on outcomes.
Analysis and Key Takeaways
	There are numerous takeaways from the interview conducted with Principal M, especially when it comes to dealing with special education students, overall student discipline, and dealing with personnel issues.  With careful consideration and handling situations with intentionality, an administrator can successfully navigate all these situations and limit the liability one suffers from disregarding rights and legislation.  One may not be able to please all parties involved all the time, but considering the rights of students and ethically handling personnel issues can be accomplished. ￼
	Regarding special education students, many laws exist to protect their rights and educational needs.  This may not always be the easiest thing to remember when one is dealing with issues that manifest from a student’s disability.  The very reason they have accommodations and protections in the first place is to receive support for these challenges they face.  If a student is not present to receive the services guaranteed to them, then one can see the disparity created when disciplinary issues keep them from those supports.  The main takeaway is that one needs to develop a heart of compassion for students as well as the rights that are afforded them through SPED services.  
	Another takeaway is that it is imperative administration take due diligence when it comes to handling all school disciplinary cases.  Many times, one may feel a knee-jerk reaction when confronted with a disciplinary situation that if not handled properly, may violate a student’s right to education by placing them out of the educational environment through suspension.  Yes, there are serious situations that alternative placements must take place through the disciplinary process.  For example, students possessing weapons or narcotics on campus are extreme situations in which the decisive action to be taken is most likely spelled out in the school’s handbook.  However, even in these situations, due process must be maintained.  In educational settings, it is imperative to interview potential eyewitnesses, gather evidence, review video footage (if available) and inform students correctly of their alleged wrongdoing and potential consequences in all disciplinary cases.  It will also behoove administrators to seek input from superiors if any vague questions remain after an investigation has occurred.  
	Finally, dealing with unwanted behaviors and attitudes of faculty and staff that have been placed under an administrator’s supervision can be tricky ground to navigate.  Having an understanding of expectations that is clearly communicated to faculty and staff is imperative.  Communication is the key component that helps to eliminate issues before they arise.  Administrators and teachers should seek to have healthy dialogue about expectations each school year on procedures and expectations.  A key takeaway here is that communication must take place before, during, and after unwanted behavior by faculty.  Although there is no way to subtract the human emotional element when it comes to disciplining faculty, one must remember that they are the key to success of all the students that they teach and are valuable resources to the school.  Managing employees with positivity and communicating exact expectations can eliminate many accusations of harassment that could be filed. 
	In conclusion, school law and ethics must be on the administrators mind when conducting business from day to day.  Although Principal Miller was only tasked to speak about three areas of concern it became obvious that this was simply the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the ever-changing landscape of school legislation.  New laws such as installing a gate between car riders and the vehicle lane and teachers wearing fluorescent vests while on duty can be overlooked if one does not stay abreast of the most current regulations.  This is both a challenge and a chore but is critical to school success and assists in remaining litigation free.  It this regard, administrative professionals must remain students themselves and actively educate themselves on current and upcoming changes in educational law.  One should never find themselves in a position of not knowing the rights of the people that they serve.  
	After speaking with Principal M, it became immediately apparent that it is not just enough for administrators to know the law, but they have to become champions and advocates for the educational rights due to each student that attends one’s school.  If there are laws that might seem nonsensical or irrelevant to an administrator, one still cannot pick and choose which law to follow and which to disregard.  This helps to protect the student, the teacher, the administrator and the school board administration.  Ultimately, administration should be the champion for all students in their care.  Administrators should keep abreast of historical court cases that highlight laws and rights that have been breached in the past as well as keep abreast of changes in the law that occur each year.  By doing so, one is less likely to find themselves inadvertently uncompliant with student and faculty rights and ethics.

According to the NBC news article published just over two years ago, a substitute teacher in north Louisiana was accused of offering three students $5 each to “tackle” a specific student during the P.E. class she was teaching.  The students allegedly took her up on the deal and took the student to the ground.  The teacher reportedly sat in the bleachers while the student that was attacked lay on the ground.  Reports were made to administrators who subsequently fired the substitute teacher and contacted local authorities.  The teacher was charged with 5 counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and malfeasance in office.  This situation is tied directly to the responsibilities of school administrators.
Current school laws are quite strict when it comes to child abuse.  It is imperative that school personnel are trained in what conduct is permissible and not tolerated.  Time and time again, the textbook (and common sense) refers to the need for establishing well-written policies, teaching them to faculty and staff, and holding periodic refresher meetings on their content.  
Although not used as a blank slate for dismissal, tenured teachers can be dismissed for “good cause.” (Section C, Chapter 1, C10) In this case, this egregious act is clearly in violation of the “neglect of duties” of the teacher and could be the impetus for termination.  There are many things to consider when terminating teacher employment but intentionally putting a student in harm’s way would rise to meeting the level of “good cause” as far as letting them go.
Depending on various conditions, the school could remain liable for damages incurred by the student that was targeted if it was found to be a contributor to the causation of the injury (Section C, Chapter 6, C109).  

In this case, I as an administrator, would take the following steps:
Before the infraction:
1.	Have a clear written policy on acceptable conduct by employees.
2.	Hold annual training on the policies and periodic refresher meetings.
Upon learning of the infraction:
1.	Immediately remove the accused from supervising students (another administrator or teacher can supervise in the meantime).
2.	Launch an immediate and in-depth investigation of the incident, including collecting recorded statements from all witnesses, perpetrators, and victims.
3.	Consult supervisors and if appropriate, law enforcement agencies.
4.	Make sure that employee disciplinary procedures are being consistently followed. 
After the investigation
1.	Work with school board supervisors to determine the employment status of the offender.
2.	Review policies to make processes clear and retrain teachers and staff.  
3.	Make sure detailed documentation is kept on file in case it is needed for litigation that may occur further down the line.
Statement of Purpose:  My purpose of this video is to capture my reflections on the things that I have learned in this course
1.	How important it is to KNOW the law
2.	How to properly APPLY the law
3.	What this looks like in the real world (in other words, what does this look as I take up this mantle of responsibility)

1.	 How important it is to KNOW the law.
a.	There is a significant saying that goes like this “Ignorance of the law is no excuse”  
b.	Administrators must make it a priority to research laws and keep themselves updated every year on educational law changes
c.	Handling situations without considering legal issues carry a lot of consequences.
i.	Louisiana is a very litigious state!  Look at all the billboards for lawyers!
ii.	Above that, we want what is fair for the student and parent.  If they are entitled to certain protections, then we must do our best to afford them those protections.
2.	 How to APPLY the law
a.	It’s not enough to know the law, an administrator has to have the proper ethics in order to apply the law equilaterally across the board.  
i.	In other words, there is no place for favoritism when it comes to policy. 
ii.	You can’t treat one student one way and the other another.  
3.	Finally, my favorite part is applying this in the real world.
a.	The principal interview we held this semester really opened my eyes to how every decision needs to filtered through the lens of the law.  
b.	A daunting task, but something that makes it easier to apply, is to create a comprehensive, but concise student handbook that contains policies that line up strategically with the current legislation.  
i.	Having this resource at your fingertips makes research quick on an administrators part and helps everyone know what legal issues apply to students, parents and faculty alike.

AHA moments:
	The little things matter:  My interview with the principal from Fairview High School really showed me how little things that are easily overlooked can be huge issues if not taken care of.  Principal M told me that at the beginning of the year they needed to buy a “gate” and cones to separate their car riders from the traffic lanes and the school also had to purchase neon traffic vests for teachers on duty to wear as they helped students to their cars.  This was a law enacted in the summer that wasn’t necessarily communicated to everyone, but adjustments needed to be made to stay in compliance.
My perspective on the law has changed since being in administration of ABC UNIVERSITY, but this course has brought a much deeper appreciation of needing to know more!

Personal and Professional Growth:
1.	Having been a faculty member in a public school, I can say that the legal ramifications of the day to day issues faced in the classroom almost seem irrelevant as a teacher. 
a.	This course really shed light on not only the DUTY of making sure student rights are upheld, but also showed the penalty for NOT doing so.  
b.	Professionally it has been a wake up call to take these matters seriously.
c.	I actually look forward now to preserving the rights of students and staying up to date on the latest issues in educational law.
Challenges
1. The most obvious challenge for me was having a major eye surgery right smack dab in the middle of the semester.  Not a lot of fun!  But I was able to work a bit ahead and get assignments in before the procedure, and thanks to the grace of some awesome professors, I was able to catch back up on assignments I was behind on.  
I think the pattern and volume or work was quite appealing and just right for this class!

Summary:
So, to sum it up, I’m very thankful for this class.  I didn’t know what to expect coming into this semester.  Law is not something that I thought I would enjoy studying, but the now, I look forward to seeing the changes that are upcoming in our department of education, even moreso now with a new presidency that is letting us know of changed in the DOE at the federal level.
I think this class has helped me to become more aware of how to shape policies that affect our students each and every day.

Chapter D2: Religious Influences and Accommodations in Public Schools

What is the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment?
prohibits the government from establishing a religion or favoring one religion over another

Court case Lemon v. Kurtzman established what?
 It gave a three part test to determine and evaluate establishment clause claims

What are the three parts Lemon Test?
#1 it must have a secular purpose  #2 a primary effect that neither advances nor impedes religion, #3 it must avoid excessive governmental entanglement with religion.

What does the law state about silent prayer in public schools?
Students can pray silently in public schools without a doubt. Legal challenges in this area have focused on state laws or school board policies that authorize a period of silent meditation or prayer in public schools.  The court pretty much leaves it alone unless it propagates religion in some form

What does the law state about meditation or silent activity?
The courts agreed that asylum activity is a good way to start the day, but draws a line at the activity furthering a religious agenda.

What does the law state about…
voluntary devotionals?
In the 1960's the Supreme Court barred daily Bible reading and prayer that was sponsored by public schools. Since then federal courts have struck down several state laws and school board policies authorizing voluntary student participation and prayers in public school assemblies and classrooms they reasoned that it violated the establishment clause

devotionals initiated by private actors?
This is sort of a mixed bag. Since school districts could not hold prayer in things such as graduation ceremonies, they changed the ceremonies into a form for student expression. Under these circumstances, the student LED devotionals at these events do not represent the public school. By and large the courts uphold this because they reason the policy was permissible since student speakers were selected based on secular criteria which is their academic standing, and we're not encouraged by school personnel to include the devotionals in their remarks. However students cannot proselyte during graduation speeches and can only talk about their own beliefs. Even then student LED devotionals and being voted on whether they should have them at school can sometimes get tricky as well.
 
What does the law state about…
proselytization by school employees or students?
The court is pretty much against this. They've gone as far as to eliminate classroom devotionals, and removing religiously oriented materials from classroom decorations. They've also made teachers cover evangelistic T-shirts they may be prayer.

religious displays, music, holiday observances?
This is also very contentious. Certain religious practices such as nativity scenes have been eliminated in certain schools Christmas songs were not allowed to be song. However on the other hand it was required to put in God we trust on the walls, as well as the 10 commandments.

What is the Equal Access Act?
 If a federally assisted public secondary school provides a limited open forum for non-curriculum student groups to meet during non-instructional time comma it cannot deny access to specific student groups because of their religious comma political comma or philosophical content of their meetings period

What does the law state about distribution of religious literature and gifts?
Most courts have prohibited school personnel and religious groups from distributing bibles. They are more open to students distributing this literature than others. Groups such as the gideons have been allowed to do Bible dissemination, however it was determined that they are not actors of the school. They usually let them do high schools because high schoolers are intelligent enough to understand they are not part of the school system and are private religious organizations.

What happen in the Eighth Circuit court case with the Gideons distribution of Bibles?
They denied them access to the elementary schools, but did allow them to go into high schools because the students were deemed intelligent enough to understand that the gideons were not employees of the school, and where a private religious group, and therefore would understand there was not conflict from proselytization from staff members.

What does the law say about holding graduation ceremonies in churches?
Contractual arrangements that are purely proprietary may be upheld if challenged under the Establishment Clause, but school authorities need to be careful that they are not selecting the venue that will be viewed as proselytizing students

How does the law allow for accommodations for religious beliefs with regards to…
release-time programs?
The court has held that the school can accommodate religion by releasing students to receive such sectarian education off of public school grounds.

religious exemptions from secular activities?
Not being forced to recite the Pledge of Allegiance, or take vaccinations have been normally upheld by the court system


What are the results of the religious challenges to curriculum with regards to…
origin of humanity?
The famous scopes monkey trial in Tennessee in 1927 upheld a law that prohibited the teaching of any theory that denies the genesis version of creation or suggests that a man has been descended from a lower order of animals period he had in 1968 the US struck down and arkansas anti evolution statute under the establishment clause

teaching evolution?
Have determined that evolution is science rather than a secular religion and says that states cannot restrict student access to such information simply to satisfy religious preferences

teaching creation and intelligent design?
Can be accepted in certain situations but the court system essentially says that intelligent design is yeah designed to inject religion into science and so they're not in favor of it.

What's interesting about this entire situation is that evolution is not considered a form of religion. Chapter C5: Evaluations

What are the goals and functions of teacher evaluation?
An appropriately conducted evaluation process facilitates open honest and effective communication between the supervisor and the employee, making clear the supervisor's expectations for job performance and the supervisors and methods of evaluating that jobs performance. The evaluation process then provides the employee with notice of strengths weaknesses and required improvements in job performance. It may also provide timelines for corrections of behaviors methods by which behavior must be corrected. This notice then becomes an effective tool to manage employee behavior. In the vast majority of cases, the outcome of an appropriate evaluation system is improved employee performance.

Written evaluations have become critical evidence when employers must justify adverse employment decisions in court. It is becoming more common for state statutes to require that employment termination and contract renewal decisions be based on  written evaluations that point out specific job performance  deficiencies, and for courts to overturn  termination decisions when evaluations are either not provided or are improperly provided.

What does the state of West Virginia’s statute state about:
The purpose for the evaluation system? First it will serve as a basis for the improvement of the performance of the personnel and their assigned duties. Second it will provide an indicator for satisfactory performance for individual professionals. Third it will serve as documentation for a dismissal on the grounds of unsatisfactory performance. And 4th it will serve as the basis for programs to increase the professional growth and development of professional personnel.
A plan for performance improvement? A professional whose performance is considered to be unsatisfactory shall be given notice of deficiencies. A remediation plan to correct deficiencies shall be developed by their employing county Board of Education and the professional. The professionals shall be given a reasonable period of time for remediating the deficiencies and you'll receive a statement of the resources and assistance available for the purposes of correcting the deficiencies.
A plan for lack of improvement? Any professional whose performance evaluation includes a written improvement plan shall be given an opportunity to improve his or her performance through the implementation of the plan. If the next performance evaluation shows that the professional is now performing satisfactorily, no further action may be taken concerning the original performance evaluation. If the evaluation shows that the professional is still not performing satisfactorily, the evaluator shall make additional recommendations for improvement or may recommend the dismissal of the professional in accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of this article.


For a principal, according to the courts, what does “substantial compliance” mean? A principal must comply with required procedures however the idea of substantial compliance attempts to avoid placing an undue burden on the school administrator. The standard of substantial compliance as opposed to full and complete compliance…

What does 2015 ESSA say about teacher evaluations? Leaves more decisions about the content of teacher and principal evaluations to the states. It does however provide that school districts may include a rigorous transparent and fair evaluation and support system for teachers principals or other school leaders that is based in part on evidence of student achievement which may include student growth and shall include multiple measures of educator performance and provide clear timely and useful feedback to teachers principals or other school leaders

What should a remediation plan include? The remediation plan should note this specific deficiencies that are being targeted, methods by which the employee can remediate the specific job performance areas, and objective criteria for determining whether or not the employee has accomplished the goal of remediating his or her job performance. Finally a remediation plan should include a timeline for remediation of the performance.

Chapter C6: Student Injury

What are torts?  Civil wrongs stemming from the unreasonable conduct of one individual resulting in another individual's personal injury property damage or reputable harm

What are principals expected to do to minimize potential tort liability for student injuries?  Effective implementation and enforcement of school policies and procedures for example school districts have implemented student discipline policies and anti bullying policies is an attempt to prevent student injuries

Define the three overarching categories of torts?
Negligence: the conduct of school personnel unintentionally fails to meet a reasonable standard of care
Intentional:  include assault and battery false imprisonment and intentional infliction of emotional distress
Defamation: injury to one's reputation generally through libel and or slander

What are the four elements needed to prove a negligence claim?
1. The plaintiff must demonstrate that the school owes a particular duty to the injured students
2. The duty must be breached by the failure to exercise an appropriate standard of care
3. The negligent conduct must be the proximate cause of the injury
4. An actual injury must occur

What is duty of care? Reasonable supervision of students through employees such as principals acting within the scope of their employment

Why do public school teachers face more restrictions with regards to academic freedom? 
1. Public employee status and contractual duty to carry out a local school board's mandates

How did these court cases shape teachers’ academic freedom and censorship?

Pickering v. Board of Education of Township High School District 205
The court ruled that teachers speech in the form of a letter to a newspaper was entitled to 1st amendment protection. The court held that a teacher cannot be discharged or otherwise punished for speaking out on issues of public concern.

Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District
The court proclaimed that neither students nor teachers shed their constitutional rights of freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate. And declared that that interference with those rights could be justified only on the basis of material and substantial disruption.

Mt. Health City School District Board of Education v. Doyle
The Supreme Court has expressly recognized that other legitimate reasons can exist for disciplining teachers who are exercising their constitutional rights this decision established the required approach for deciding such cases. First the teacher has the burden of showing that constitutionally protected conduct was a motivating factor in the teacher's discharge or other school disciplinary action. If so the burden shifts to the school officials to prove that they would have followed the same course of action in the absence of protected conduct. The court made it clear that speech of public concern is protected speech, even though it may be expressed privately by an employee to a supervisor.

Garcetti v. Ceballos
The First Amendment does not protect a public employee whose statements are made pursuant to official duties rather than as a private citizen
